<p class="paper-meta">First Author · Submitted Manuscript</p>

## Abstract

<p class="abstract-text">Scientific talent mobility is an important force shaping the global innovation landscape. Existing studies, however, have largely explained talent mobility from a whole-network perspective, emphasizing urban science and innovation conditions and multidimensional proximity, while paying insufficient attention to individual career trajectories and the supporting role of research platforms. Using career histories, research outputs, and urban attribute data for top global biomedical scientists from 1970 to 2023, this study combines social network analysis, weighted exponential random graph models, and ego-network analysis to examine the structural characteristics, formation mechanisms, and individual mobility processes of their intercity mobility network. The results show that: (1) The intercity mobility network of top global biomedical scientists exhibits a low-density, highly selective core–periphery structure. Its European and North American core and transatlantic connections remain broadly stable, while cities specializing in medical research, biomedical research and development, and related industrial activities become increasingly prominent in later periods. (2) Intercity mobility ties among top global biomedical scientists are jointly shaped by endogenous network structure, urban science and innovation conditions, and multidimensional proximity. Geographical distance consistently constrains mobility, whereas institutional proximity consistently facilitates it. The effect of cultural proximity weakens in the later period, while cognitive proximity shows no stable association. The effects of urban science and innovation conditions vary across periods and between origins and destinations: specialized research platforms explain mobility more consistently than general economic scale. The initial stock of cross-platform embedded talent is significantly associated with subsequent mobility ties, with a more stable association at the origin. (3) Ego-network analysis shows that the intercity mobility of top global biomedical scientists is a cross-scale spatial process jointly shaped by network structure, urban conditions, multidimensional proximity, historical ties, and individual career trajectories.</p>
